name: Propositional Logic
description: Connectives, truth tables, logical equivalences and the valid argument forms built on them.

questions.question: The statement "If the server is down, the alert fires" is evaluated on a day when the server is NOT down and no alert fires. What is the truth value of the implication?
options: False, because the alert never fired
It cannot be determined without more information
True, because a false antecedent makes the implication true
True, but only because both parts are false
questions.explain: An implication P → Q is false only in the single case where P is true and Q is false. With P false the implication is vacuously true, regardless of Q. The last option gets the right answer for the wrong reason: it would still be true if the alert had fired.

questions.question: What is the contrapositive of "If it rains, the match is cancelled"?
options: If the match is not cancelled, then it did not rain
If the match is cancelled, then it rained
If it does not rain, then the match is not cancelled
It rains and the match is not cancelled
questions.explain: The contrapositive of P → Q is ¬Q → ¬P, and it is always logically equivalent to the original. The second option is the converse and the third is the inverse; neither is equivalent to the original statement.

questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to ¬(P ∧ Q)?
options: ¬P ∧ ¬Q
P ∨ Q
¬P ∧ Q
¬P ∨ ¬Q
questions.explain: De Morgan's law: negating a conjunction turns it into a disjunction of the negated parts. The first option is the classic mistake of distributing the negation without flipping the connective, and it is equivalent to ¬(P ∨ Q) instead.

questions.question: A formula that evaluates to true under every possible assignment of its variables is called:
options: A contingency
A tautology
A contradiction
A satisfiable formula
questions.explain: A tautology is true under every assignment. Every tautology is also satisfiable, but satisfiable only requires at least one true assignment, so it is the weaker property and not the answer here.

questions.question: How many rows does a complete truth table for a formula with 4 distinct propositional variables have?
questions.explain: Each variable is independently true or false, so the table has 2^n rows: 2^4 = 16. The answer 8 is 2^3, a common off-by-one when the variables are miscounted.

questions.question: You know that "If the build passes, the artifact is published" is true, and you observe that the artifact was NOT published. What follows?
options: The build did not pass
The build passed
Nothing follows about the build
The build both passed and failed
questions.explain: This is modus tollens: from P → Q and ¬Q you may conclude ¬P. If the build had passed, the artifact would necessarily have been published.

questions.question: From "If the disk is full, writes fail" and the observation "writes are failing", a colleague concludes the disk is full. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Nothing, this is modus ponens
The implication should have been negated first
The premises contradict each other
It affirms the consequent, which is an invalid form
questions.explain: From P → Q and Q you cannot conclude P, because Q may have other causes (bad permissions, a read-only mount). Modus ponens requires observing the antecedent P, not the consequent Q.

questions.question: Which expression is logically equivalent to P → Q?
options: P ∧ ¬Q
¬P ∨ Q
¬P ∧ Q
P ∨ ¬Q
questions.explain: The implication is false only when P is true and Q is false, which is exactly the negation of P ∧ ¬Q, that is ¬P ∨ Q. Note that P ∧ ¬Q is the negation of the implication, not an equivalent of it.

questions.question: What can be said about the formula P ∧ ¬P?
options: It is a contradiction and therefore unsatisfiable
It is a tautology by the law of excluded middle
It is true whenever P is true
It is satisfiable but not a tautology
questions.explain: No assignment makes both P and ¬P true, so the formula is false everywhere. The law of excluded middle is P ∨ ¬P, the disjunction, which is the tautology and is easy to confuse with this one.

questions.question: The biconditional P ↔ Q is true exactly when:
options: Both P and Q are true
At least one of P and Q is true
P and Q have the same truth value
P is true and Q is false
questions.explain: P ↔ Q holds when both are true and also when both are false, since it abbreviates (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P). Requiring both to be true describes conjunction, which misses the false-false row.
